linear-operator-linearity-identity-1-a1d.title: Linear Operator Superposition Mapping
linear-operator-linearity-identity-1-a1d.interpretation:
The equation 
$$ \hat{A}(c_1|\psi\rangle + c_2|\phi\rangle) = c_1\hat{A}|\psi\rangle + c_2\hat{A}|\phi\rangle $$
 demonstrates the linearity of the operator 

$\hat{A}$\n. Here, 

$|\psi\rangle$\n and 

$|\phi\rangle$\n represent two arbitrary quantum states (vectors in a Hilbert space), and 

$c_1$\n and 

$c_2$\n are complex scalar coefficients representing the weights of each state in a superposition. The left side of the equation shows the operator 

$\hat{A}$\n acting on the combined state 

$(c_1|\psi\rangle + c_2|\phi\rangle)$\n. The right side shows that this is equivalent to applying the operator 

$\hat{A}$\n to each state individually (

$\hat{A}|\psi\rangle$\n and 

$\hat{A}|\phi\rangle)$\n and then taking the same linear combination of the results, scaled by the original coefficients 

$c_1$\n and 

$c_2$\n. This property is fundamental to the behavior of quantum mechanical observables, which are represented by linear operators.
linear-operator-linearity-identity-1-a1d.symmetry_origin: The linearity of operators is a fundamental postulate in quantum mechanics, stemming from the vector space structure of Hilbert spaces and the requirement that physical observables correspond to linear transformations that preserve the probabilistic interpretation of quantum states.
linear-operator-linearity-identity-1-a1d.limits_and_boundary: This equation holds true for any pair of quantum states $|\psi\rangle, |\phi\rangle$ and any complex coefficients $c_1, c_2$. The operator $\hat{A}$ can be any linear operator (e.g., a Hamiltonian, momentum operator, position operator).  In the limit where $c_1=0$, the equation reduces to $\hat{A}(c_2|\phi\rangle) = c_2\hat{A}|\phi\rangle$, showing the scaling property of linear operators. If $c_2=0$, it reduces to the same property for the state $|\psi\rangle$. If $|\psi\rangle = |\phi\rangle$, the equation becomes $\hat{A}((c_1+c_2)|\psi\rangle) = (c_1+c_2)\hat{A}|\psi\rangle$, again illustrating homogeneity.

\\hat{A}.name: Operator A
\\hat{A}.description: A linear operator representing a physical observable or a transformation in a quantum mechanical system. It acts on quantum states.

|\\psi\\rangle.name: Quantum State Psi
|\\psi\\rangle.description: An arbitrary quantum state vector in a Hilbert space, representing the state of a quantum system.

|\\phi\\rangle.name: Quantum State Phi
|\\phi\\rangle.description: Another arbitrary quantum state vector in a Hilbert space, representing the state of a quantum system.

c_1.name: Complex Coefficient 1
c_1.description: A complex scalar coefficient that scales the quantum state |\psi\rangle in a superposition.

c_2.name: Complex Coefficient 2
c_2.description: A complex scalar coefficient that scales the quantum state |\phi\rangle in a superposition.

linear-operator-linearity-identity-1-a1d.conceptual_definition: This formula illustrates the principle of superposition for linear operators in quantum mechanics. It states that a linear operator, when acting on a linear combination of two quantum states, produces a result that is the same linear combination of the operator acting on each state individually.
linear-operator-linearity-identity-1-a1d.intuitive_summary: Linear operators respect superpositions of quantum states, meaning they act on each part of the superposition independently and then recombine the results.

loschmidts-paradox-identity-1-86c06f22-2.title: The Time-Reversal Symmetry of Classical Equations
loschmidts-paradox-identity-1-86c06f22-2.interpretation: The transformation vec{T}vec{: t \to -t, \quad \mathbf{r}(t) \to \mathbf{r}(-t), \quad \mathbf{p}(t) \to -\mathbf{p}(-t)} describes how the coordinates and momentum of a particle transform under a time-reversal operation. Specifically, time itself is reversed, meaning that a state at time $t$ evolves to the same state at time $-t$. The position vector vec{r}(t) at time $t$ becomes the position vector vec{r}(-t) at the reversed time, which is equivalent to the position vector at the original time $t$ but traced backwards along the trajectory. Crucially, the linear momentum vec{p}(t), defined as the product of mass and velocity (vec{p} = mvec{v}), must change its sign. Since velocity vec{v} = dvec{r}/dt, reversing time means vec{v}(-t) = dvec{r}(-t)/d(-t) = -dvec{r}(-t)/dt. If vec{r}(-t) is the position at time $-t$, then vec{v}(-t) points in the opposite direction of vec{v}(t). For the laws of motion, such as Newton's second law vec{F} = dvec{p}/dt, to remain invariant, the momentum must flip its sign under time reversal. This is because the acceleration, which is the second derivative of position with respect to time (vec{a} = d^2vec{r}/dt^2), remains unchanged under time reversal (vec{a}(-t) = d^2vec{r}(-t)/d(-t)^2 = d^2vec{r}(-t)/dt^2 = vec{a}(t)). If vec{F} = mvec{a} is to be invariant, and vec{a} is invariant, then vec{F} must be invariant. Since vec{F} = dvec{p}/dt, and reversing time means d/dt becomes d/d(-t) = -d/dt, for vec{F} to be invariant, vec{p} must change sign.
loschmidts-paradox-identity-1-86c06f22-2.symmetry_origin: The time-reversal symmetry arises from the fact that the fundamental equations of motion in classical mechanics, such as Newton's second law (vec{F} = mvec{a}), are differential equations of second order in time. When considering the transformation vec{t} \to -vec{t}, the second derivative vec{a} = d^2vec{r}/dt^2 is invariant: d^2vec{r}/dt^2 = d^2vec{r}/d(-vec{t})^2. If the forces vec{F} depend only on position and velocity (e.g., velocity-independent forces like gravity, or velocity-dependent forces like the Lorentz force where vec{v} flips sign and the magnetic field vec{B} is assumed to be time-independent), then the equation of motion vec{F}(vec{r}, vec{v}) = mvec{a} transforms to vec{F}(vec{r}(-t), -vec{v}(-t)) = mvec{a}(-t). For time-reversal symmetry, we require vec{F}(vec{r}(-t), -vec{v}(-t)) = vec{F}(vec{r}(t), vec{v}(t)), which, coupled with the invariance of acceleration, ensures the symmetry.
loschmidts-paradox-identity-1-86c06f22-2.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where time approaches infinity (vec{t} \to \pm\infty), the concept of time reversal essentially describes the behavior of a system 'going back' to a past state. For systems governed by classical mechanics without dissipative forces (like friction), time-reversal symmetry implies that if a system evolves from state A to state B, it can also evolve from state B to state A by reversing the velocities. However, in the presence of friction or other dissipative forces, which are typically modeled as velocity-dependent forces that oppose motion, time-reversal symmetry is broken. These forces cause systems to lose energy over time, leading to an irreversible increase in entropy, and running the movie backward would show energy spontaneously appearing, which is unphysical.

t.name: Time
t.description: The independent variable representing time, which is reversed in the transformation.

\\mathbf{r}(t).name: Position Vector
\\mathbf{r}(t).description: The vector indicating the position of a particle or system in space as a function of time.

\\mathbf{p}(t).name: Linear Momentum Vector
\\mathbf{p}(t).description: The vector quantity representing the mass in motion, defined as mass times velocity (vec{p} = mvec{v}). It reverses direction under time reversal.

\\mathcal{T}.name: Time Reversal Operator
\\mathcal{T}.description: The operator that performs the time-reversal transformation.

loschmidts-paradox-identity-1-86c06f22-2.conceptual_definition: The time-reversal symmetry of classical mechanics dictates that the fundamental laws of motion remain unchanged if the direction of time is reversed, provided that the initial velocities are also reversed. This implies that the future and past are, in principle, indistinguishable from the perspective of the fundamental equations.
loschmidts-paradox-identity-1-86c06f22-2.intuitive_summary: If you were to run a movie of a classical physical system backwards, it would still look like a valid physical process obeying the same laws.
